analysis.one_liner: Licenses opioid drug salespeople, pulls ultra-high-dose opioids off the market, and taxes opioid makers to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of the four committees it was sent to, and it died when the 115th Congress ended with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have attacked the opioid epidemic at the supply side. It would require drug-company salespeople who promote strong opioids to get a federal license with ethics training, force the FDA to pull ultra-high-dose opioids off the market, require doctors to get training before prescribing, and impose a 1-cent-per-milligram tax on opioid manufacturers. Half the tax money would fund a national program for safely disposing of leftover pills, and the other half would fund substance abuse treatment through federal grants. It also would create public maps of opioid prescribing in Medicaid and study whether Medicare should cover non-drug pain treatments like acupuncture and exercise therapy.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of opioid addiction, patients who need addiction treatment, and communities dealing with leftover pills. The tax on manufacturers would directly fund treatment grants and a national take-back program for unused opioids.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of addiction and their communities

how_it_helps.text: Half of the new 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on opioid manufacturers would fund substance abuse treatment block grants; the other half would fund a national take-back program requiring at least one safe disposal site per 25,000 residents.

Starting in 2020, anyone who markets schedule II opioids on behalf of a manufacturer for more than 15 days a year would need a federal license costing $3,000, with certified training in ethics and the CDC opioid guidelines, and annual reports naming every provider visited and every gift or sample given.

Any 'ultra-high-dose' opioid — one whose label exceeds the daily limits in the CDC prescribing guidelines — would automatically be treated as an imminent public health hazard and have its FDA approval suspended.

Doctors registering or renewing with the DEA to prescribe controlled substances would have to certify they completed opioid training, or limit themselves to 72-hour supplies, and register with their state's prescription monitoring database.

The bill would require a public mapping tool showing opioid prescribing by Medicaid providers down to the ZIP code, and would open the DEA's shipment-tracking database (ARCOS) to state medical and pharmacy boards.

It would commission a National Academy of Medicine study on whether Medicare should cover non-drug pain treatments such as acupuncture, exercise therapy, and biofeedback for back pain, since lack of coverage may push patients toward opioids.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, who would pay the new excise tax on every milligram of active opioid they produce, and their sales forces, who would face licensing fees, training, and disclosure requirements. Patients might also bear some costs through higher drug prices and tighter prescribing limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid manufacturers and their sales forces

drawbacks.text: The bill would let state law enforcement agencies directly access prescription monitoring databases and would require states to send HHS and the DEA lists of every practitioner and dispenser who prescribed opioids and how much — raising privacy concerns for legitimate patients and doctors.

Doctors who did not complete the required training could only prescribe a 72-hour supply with no refills, and the bill's own GAO-study provision acknowledges the need to avoid cutting off patients 'who need such opioids' — chronic pain patients and their doctors warned that blunt supply restrictions can hurt people who take opioids responsibly.
A per-milligram tax on manufacturers would likely be passed through to drug prices, and patients who depend on these medications would bear part of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade the bill makes is real: drug manufacturers and sales practices were central to the oversupply of opioids, and the bill makes them pay for treatment and disposal while tightening prescribing. The heaviest burden falls on the industry that created the product, not on patients. The main risks are on the access side — automated suspension of high-dose opioids and a strict 72-hour default could squeeze chronic pain patients, and expanded law-enforcement access to prescription data raises privacy issues. On balance, the design aims the costs at the industry and the benefits at treatment, prevention, and safer disposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2018 and referred to four House committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — then to two subcommittees, but no committee ever held a hearing or scheduled a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on May 17, 2018 with no cosponsors.

The Speaker sent it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — a multi-committee referral that makes passage harder because any one committee can hold a bill.

By June and July 2018 it had been referred to the Health Subcommittee and the Crime subcommittee, but the action record shows no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

Congress did pass a broad opioids package (the SUPPORT Act) later in 2018, but this bill's manufacturer excise tax, sales-rep licensing, and automatic withdrawal of ultra-high-dose opioids did not become law in it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers came out ahead: because the bill never moved, they avoided the 1-cent-per-milligram tax, the sales-rep licensing regime, and the automatic suspension of ultra-high-dose products. People seeking treatment gained nothing from it, though federal treatment funding continued through existing programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who avoided the tax

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Addiction Prevention and Responsible Opioid Practices Act on May 17, 2018.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan split is recorded; the sponsor was a Democrat from Pennsylvania, an opioid-affected state.

industries.note: The bill would tax every milligram of active opioid they produce at 1 cent, license and surveil their sales reps, and automatically suspend approval of ultra-high-dose products. The industry's interest in blocking it ran against the public's interest in treatment funding and safer prescribing.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical sales and marketing (opioid sales reps)
industries.note: Reps promoting schedule II opioids would need a $3,000 federal license, certified ethics and CDC-guideline training, and annual reports naming every provider visited and every gift or sample given — ending the loose gift-and-samples culture that helped drive overprescribing.
Half the excise tax revenue would flow to SAMHSA treatment block grants and related programs, expanding paid treatment capacity. Their interest ran alongside patients'.

Prescribers would face mandatory training, prescription-database checks, reporting duties, and potential 72-hour dispensing limits — added paperwork and legal exposure, but also clearer standards and liability cover for responsible prescribing.
